main.title: Neon Genesis Evangelion
main.summary: Neon Genesis Evangelion began broadcasting in October 1995, directed by Hideaki Anno and produced by Gainax and Tatsunoko.

cards.heading: Neon Genesis Evangelion
cards.text: Neon Genesis Evangelion began broadcasting in October 1995, directed by Hideaki Anno and produced by Gainax and Tatsunoko. In a fortified Tokyo-3 after a global catastrophe, teenager Shinji Ikari joins Nerv at his father's request. He pilots a giant biomechanical Evangelion against beings called Angels. The battles lead into the emotional experiences of the pilots and the motives of the organisation around them. Religious and mystical imagery accompanies those questions. The series uses the familiar scale of a mecha story to explore anxiety, relationships and the pressures placed on its young characters.

main.title: Toy Story
main.summary: Toy Story is a 1995 American animated adventure comedy film directed by John Lasseter, and written by Joss Whedon, Andrew Stanton, Joel Cohen, and Alec Sokolow.

cards.heading: Toy Story
cards.text:
Toy Story is a 1995 American animated adventure comedy film directed by John Lasseter, and written by Joss Whedon, Andrew Stanton, Joel Cohen, and Alec Sokolow. The first entirely computer-animated feature film, as well as the first feature film produced by Pixar Animation Studios for Walt Disney Pictures, it stars the voices of Tom Hanks, Tim Allen, Annie Potts, John Ratzenberger, Don Rickles, Wallace Shawn, and Jim Varney. Set in a world in which toys come to life, Toy Story follows an old-fashioned cowboy doll named Woody (Hanks), who becomes jealous that a space cadet action figure, Buzz Lightyear (Allen), is replacing him as the favorite toy of their owner Andy.

Following the success of the 1988 short film Tin Toy, Pixar was approached by Disney to produce a computer-animated feature film that was told from a small toy's perspective. Lasseter, Stanton, and Pete Docter wrote early story treatments, which were rejected by Disney, who wanted the film's tone to be edgier.

main.title: Windows 95
main.summary: Windows 95  is a consumer-oriented operating system developed by Microsoft, released to manufacturing on July 14, 1995, and to retail on August 24, 1995.

cards.heading: Windows 95
cards.text:
Windows 95  is a consumer-oriented operating system developed by Microsoft, released to manufacturing on July 14, 1995, and to retail on August 24, 1995. The first of the Windows 9x line of operating systems, Windows 95, which replaced Windows 3.1, merged Microsoft's MS-DOS and Windows operating systems into a single product, and featured major changes to the core components of the operating system, such as moving from the mainly cooperatively multitasked 16-bit architecture of its predecessor to a 32-bit preemptive multitasking architecture.

Windows 95 featured a new graphical user interface (GUI), introducing the Windows Explorer file manager, a taskbar with the Start menu and a notification area, and file shortcuts on the desktop, and implemented a number of improvements over its predecessor, including Plug-and-Play driver integration, native Internet integration, and support for longer filenames (from 8 to 255 characters). Accompanied by an extensive marketing campaign that generated much prerelease hype, it was a major success and is regarded as one of the most significant products in the personal computing industry.

main.title: (What's the Story) Morning Glory?

main.summary: Oasis released their second album, (What's the Story) Morning Glory?, on 2 October 1995. Produced by Owen Morris and Noel Gallagher and recorded at Rockfield in Wales, it includes Wonderwall, Don't Look Back in Anger and Champagne Supernova. Its songs gave the Manchester band a broader audience while retaining the force of their guitars and direct vocal delivery.

cards.heading: A second album with a wider reach
cards.text: Oasis released their second album, (What's the Story) Morning Glory?, on 2 October 1995. Produced by Owen Morris and Noel Gallagher and recorded at Rockfield in Wales, it includes Wonderwall, Don't Look Back in Anger and Champagne Supernova. Its songs gave the Manchester band a broader audience while retaining the force of their guitars and direct vocal delivery.

cards.heading: Songs built for different voices
cards.text: Wonderwall places an acoustic rhythm beneath Liam Gallagher's voice, leaving room for a refrain that listeners can readily join. Don't Look Back in Anger gives Noel the lead vocal and begins at the piano. The title track returns to a harder guitar attack, while Champagne Supernova stretches the closing section into a slower, spacious farewell. Moving between these approaches gives the record a range of moods within a familiar band sound.

cards.heading: A London street on the sleeve
cards.text: The sleeve places the album in an ordinary city street. Producer Owen Morris and DJ Sean Rowley pass one another on Berwick Street in London, surrounded by shopfronts and a long view down the road. The image became a recognisable companion to songs heard far beyond their recording studio. Wonderwall followed as a single on 30 October 1995; the official band catalogue identifies it among their most popular songs.

main.title: Dolly
main.summary: Dolly (5 July 1996 – 14 February 2003) was a female Finn-Dorset sheep and the first mammal that was cloned from an adult somatic cell.

cards.heading: Dolly
cards.text:
Born on July 5, 1996, Dolly was a Finn-Dorset sheep and the first mammal cloned from an adult somatic cell. The Roslin Institute team in Scotland used nuclear transfer with a cell taken from a mammary gland, demonstrating that a mature cell from a specialised body part could produce a cloned organism.

The approach followed foundational work by John Gurdon on African clawed frogs in 1958. Dolly's successful cloning contributed to advances in stem-cell research, including work that led to induced pluripotent stem cells. She lived until February 14, 2003.

main.title: 3dfx Voodoo Graphics
main.summary: Voodoo Graphics brought dedicated 3D rendering hardware into PCs during the rise of 3D games.

cards.heading: 3dfx Voodoo Graphics
cards.text: Voodoo Graphics brought dedicated 3D rendering hardware into PCs during the rise of 3D games. Developed by 3dfx, the add-in card worked alongside an existing graphics card, which continued handling ordinary 2D output. Games increasingly supported 3dfx's Glide interface to use its acceleration, and Voodoo2 followed its success. The market soon moved towards cards combining 2D and 3D functions. Microsoft's Direct3D also gave developers a common interface across competing hardware, reducing the advantage of Glide. Voodoo's success helped make accelerated 3D an expected part of PC gaming.

main.title: Pilot 1000
main.summary: The Pilot 1000 and Pilot 5000 are the first generations of PDAs produced by Palm Computing (then a subsidiary of USRobotics).

cards.heading: Pilot 1000
cards.text:
Palm Computing introduced the Pilot 1000 and Pilot 5000 personal digital assistants in March 1996, while it was a subsidiary of USRobotics. Both used a 16 MHz Motorola 68328 processor, with 128 KB of RAM in the Pilot 1000 and 512 KB in the Pilot 5000.

The 160-by-160-pixel monochrome touchscreen reserved its lower third for Graffiti handwriting input. Four physical buttons opened the Date Book, Address Book, To Do List and Memo Pad, alongside two scrolling buttons. A stylus slotted into the top of the case, and a serial port connected the handheld to its cradle. Powered by two AAA batteries, the device weighed 160 grams.

main.title: Space Jam
main.summary: Space Jam brought Michael Jordan and the Looney Tunes together in November 1996.

cards.heading: Space Jam
cards.text: Space Jam brought Michael Jordan and the Looney Tunes together in November 1996. Playing himself, the basketball star joins the animated characters for a match against aliens who plan to turn them into amusement-park attractions. Director Joe Pytka combined live action with animation, placing the athlete inside their cartoon world. Critics disagreed about the premise, while praising aspects of the technical combination. Audiences made it a commercial success: worldwide earnings of about 250 million dollars made it the highest-grossing basketball film at the time, extending Jordan's screen presence beyond the court.

main.title: Dario Fo wins the Nobel Prize in Literature
main.summary: Dario Fo received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1997 for theatre that challenged authority and defended the dignity of oppressed people.

cards.heading: Dario Fo wins the Nobel Prize in Literature
cards.text: Dario Fo received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1997 for theatre that challenged authority and defended the dignity of oppressed people. A playwright and performer, he drew on improvisation, medieval strolling players and commedia dell'arte. Those traditions gave him ways to address contemporary politics directly through the stage. His plays criticised corruption, organised crime, racism and war, and reached audiences through translations into thirty languages. The Nobel recognised a theatrical practice in which acting, writing and public argument worked together, bringing popular performance forms into international literary recognition.

main.title: Deep Blue versus Garry Kasparov
main.summary: Garry Kasparov, then-world champion in chess, played a pair of six-game matches against Deep Blue, a supercomputer by IBM.

cards.heading: Deep Blue versus Garry Kasparov
cards.text: Garry Kasparov, then-world champion in chess, played a pair of six-game matches against Deep Blue, a supercomputer by IBM. Kasparov won the first match, held at the Pennsylvania Convention Center in Philadelphia in 1996, by 4–2. Deep Blue won a 1997 rematch, held at the Equitable Center in New York City, by 3½–2½. The second match was the first defeat of a reigning world chess champion by a computer under tournament conditions, and was the subject of a documentary film, Game Over: Kasparov and the Machine.
